This fixture lesson exercises every text and code component the MDX pipeline supports, so the
gates and the design review have real content to check against.

<Callout kind="note">
A note callout looks like this: a short aside that adds context without interrupting the main
explanation.
</Callout>

<Callout kind="warning">
A warning callout flags a common mistake before the learner makes it themselves.
</Callout>

<Callout kind="grader-tip">
A grader tip callout explains something specific to how the judge checks a submission, such as
exact output matching.
</Callout>

The term <Term id="variable">variable</Term> links to its entry in the glossary; hovering or
opening the link shows the definition inline.

<Details summary="A collapsible detail, closed by default">
This text is hidden until the learner opens it, which is useful for an optional aside that would
otherwise break up the main explanation.
</Details>

Here is a small program with two lines highlighted and a caption:

<Code file="examples/basics.py" lines="1-7" highlight="4,5" caption="Counting the letters in a greeting" />

This example shows its own committed input and output, so nothing here is typed by hand:

<Code file="examples/echo.py" showOutput caption="Summing three numbers read from standard input" />

The same output can also stand alone, without its source shown again:

<Output file="examples/echo.out" />

This example is deliberately wrong: it reads past the end of a three-item list, and the lesson
reader labels it as failing, with the real traceback PyPy 3.8 produces.

<Code file="examples/oops.py" expectError="IndexError" caption="Reading one index past the end of the list" />

A fenced block works the same way as a file-based one:

```python
values = [1, 2, 3]
print(sum(values))
```

This fenced block is deliberately not valid on Python 3.8, since the `match` statement is a
3.10 feature, so the reader marks it as failing on the grader:

```python bad38
match len([1, 2, 3]):
    case 3:
        print("three items")
    case _:
        print("some other count")
```
